column2: Om. In the delightful city of Ayodhya, in the midst of a jewelled pavilion, (sat Rama) surrounded by Sita, Bharata, Lakshmana, Shatrughna and others —
praised day and night by hosts of sages such as Sanaka, by Vasishtha and others, by Shuka and others, and by other devotees —
the witness of thousands of modifications of the mind, himself unchanging, Hari, intent on meditation on his own nature at the end of absorption.
Hanuman (Maruti), praising Rama with devotion and service, asked: "Rama, you are the Supreme Self, whose form is being, consciousness and bliss."
Now, best of the Raghus, I bow to you again and again. I wish to know your true nature, Rama, for the sake of liberation,
by which I may be freed from the bonds of worldly existence without effort. Out of compassion, tell me, Rama, that by which I shall be liberated.
(Rama said:) "Well asked, mighty-armed one. I shall tell you truly; listen. I am firmly established in the Vedanta; take refuge in the Vedanta."
(Hanuman:) "Best of the Raghus, what are the Vedantas, and where do they abide? Tell me." (Rama:) "Hanuman, listen; I shall tell you plainly the position of the Vedanta."
The Vedas, of great extent, were born as the breath of Vishnu, of me. In the Veda, like oil in sesame seeds, the Vedanta is firmly established.
(Hanuman:) "Rama, how many kinds of Vedas are there, and their branches, descendant of Raghu? And which are the Upanishads among them? Kindly tell me truly."
Sri Rama said: "By the division beginning with the Rig Veda, four Vedas are declared. Their branches are many, and so are the Upanishads among them."
Of the Rig Veda there are twenty-one branches; of the Yajus, son of the Wind, a hundred and nine branches.
Of the Sama Veda, scorcher of foes, there are a thousand branches; and of the Atharvan, Hari, there are fifty divisions.
For each branch one Upanishad is held. Whoever reads even one verse of them with devotion to me
attains the state of union with me, which is hard for sages to reach. (Hanuman:) "Rama, some of the best sages say that liberation is one;"
some say it comes through worship of your name, in Kashi, through the teaching of the saving mantra; others through Sankhya and Yoga, and others through the yoga of devotion;
other great sages through reflection on the meaning of the Vedanta texts. By the division into sharing the same world and the rest, liberation is declared fourfold.
Sri Rama said: "The liberation of isolation (kaivalya) is one alone, of ultimate nature. Even one who is given to wrong conduct, monkey, by worship of my name"
obtains the liberation of sharing my world, but not another world and the like. But one who dies in Kashi, in this lotus-stalk of Brahman, obtains me as his saviour.
That person attains a liberation free from return. Wherever in Kashi one dies, Mahesvara (Shiva)
should instruct the creature in the right ear with the saving mantra of me. Freed from the entire flood of sins, he attains likeness to me.
That is called the liberation of the same world and the same form. Being always devoted to right conduct, a twice-born of undivided mind
whose feeling for me is that of the Self of all, attains nearness to me. That is held to be the liberation of the same world, same form and nearness.
By the path taught by the teacher, meditating on my imperishable qualities, the twice-born rightly attains union with me, like the caterpillar that becomes a bee.
That is the liberation of union, auspicious, producing the bliss of Brahman. This fourfold liberation arises through worship of me.
(Hanuman:) "By what means is this liberation of isolation attained?" (Rama:) "The Mandukya alone is sufficient for the liberation of seekers of freedom."
If knowledge is still not attained, read the ten Upanishads; having gained knowledge, in a short time you will go to my abode.
If still, son of Anjana, the firmness of your knowledge is not there, practise the Upanishads of the thirty-two and remove it.
If you desire bodiless liberation, read the one hundred and eight. Listen; I shall tell you truly their order and their peace-mantras.
Isha, Kena, Katha, Prashna, Mundaka, Mandukya, Taittiriya, Aitareya, Chandogya and Brihadaranyaka;
Brahma, Kaivalya, Jabala, Shvetashvatara, Hamsa, Aruni, Garbha, Narayana, Hamsa (Paramahamsa), Bindu, Nada(bindu), Shira(s), Shikha;
Maitrayani, Kaushitaki, Brihajjabala, Tapani, Kalagnirudra, Maitreyi, Subala, Kshurika, Mantrika;
Sarvasara, Niralamba, Rahasya (Shukarahasya), Vajrasuchika, Tejobindu, Nadabindu, Dhyanabindu, Brahmavidya, Yogatattva, Atmabodha;
Parivrat (Narada-parivrajaka), Trishikhi(brahmana), Sita, Chuda(mani), Nirvana, Mandala(brahmana), Dakshina(murti), Sharabha, Skanda, and the one called Mahanarayana;
Advayataraka (Rahasya), Ramatapana, Vasudeva, Mudgala, Shandilya, Paingala, Bhikshu, Mahat (Maha), Sharirika, Shikha (Yogashikha);
Turiyatita, Sannyasa, Parivraja(ka), Akshamalika, Avyakta, Ekakshara, Purna (Annapurna), Surya, Akshi, Adhyatma, Kundika;
Savitri, Atma, Pashupata, Parabrahma, Avadhuta, Tripuratapana, Devi, Tripura, Katha(rudra), Bhavana, Hridaya, Kundalini, Bhasma, Rudraksha, Ganapati (and) Darshana;
Tarasara, Mahavakya, Pancha(brahma), Agnihotra, Gopalatapana, Krishna, Yajnavalkya, Varaha;
Shatyayani, Hayagriva, Dattatreya, Garuda, Kali(santarana), Jabali, Saubhagya(lakshmi), Rahasya (Sarasvatirahasya), Rig(veda), and Muktika.
Thus the one hundred and eight destroy the three kinds of mental conditioning; they bestow knowledge and dispassion on people and destroy the three kinds of habit-impressions.
Taking them from the mouth of a teacher who has bathed in Vedic study and vows, preceded by the respective peace-mantras prescribed in the earlier and later parts,
the best of the twice-born who read the one hundred and eight become liberated while living, until their prarabdha karma is exhausted.
Then, in due time, when their prarabdha has come to an end, they attain my bodiless liberation; there is no doubt in this.
Among all the Upanishads, the one hundred and eight are the essence; by hearing them but once, the whole flood of sins is cut away.
This has been taught by me to you, my disciple, son of the Wind. This scripture, taught by me, is the secret one hundred and eight.
For those who read it, knowingly or unknowingly, it releases from bondage. A kingdom may be given, wealth may be given, and the desire of one who asks may be fulfilled;
but this one hundred and eight should not be given to just anyone — not to an unbeliever, an ungrateful person, or one who delights in wrong conduct,
nor to one turned away from devotion to me, who is bewildered in the pits of the scriptures, nor ever to one without devotion to a teacher.
To a disciple devoted to service, Maruti, to a good son, to my devotee, of good character, of good family, of good understanding,

— after careful examination — should this one hundred and eight be given. Whoever reads or even hears it comes to me; there is no doubt. Thus it is said in the verse: "Knowledge came to the Brahmin and said: Guard me; I am your treasure. Do not give me to the envious, the crooked, the deceitful; so I shall be powerful. To the one you know as attentive to learning and hearing, wise, and devoted to chastity — to him who has approached, after careful examination, one should give this knowledge of Vishnu, the steadfastness in the Self."

Thus. Then Maruti asked Sri Ramachandra: "Tell me the separate peace-mantras according to the divisions beginning with the Rig Veda." Sri Rama said: for the ten Upanishads belonging to the Rig Veda — Aitareya, Kaushitaki, Nadabindu, Atmabodha, Nirvana, Mudgala, Akshamalika, Tripura, Saubhagya and Bahvricha — the peace-mantra is "May my speech be founded in my mind."

For the nineteen Upanishads belonging to the White Yajur Veda — Isha, Brihadaranyaka, Jabala, Hamsa, Paramahamsa, Subala, Mantrika, Niralamba, Trishikhi, Mandalabrahmana, Advayataraka, Paingala, Bhikshu, Turiyatita, Adhyatma, Tarasara, Yajnavalkya, Shatyayani and Muktika — the peace-mantra is "That is full."

For the thirty-two Upanishads belonging to the Black Yajur Veda — Katha(valli), Taittiriya, Brahma, Kaivalya, Shvetashvatara, Garbha, Narayana, Amritabindu, Amritanada, Kalagnirudra, Kshurika, Sarvasara, Shukarahasya, Tejobindu, Dhyanabindu, Brahmavidya, Yogatattva, Dakshinamurti, Skanda, Sharirika, Yogashikha, Ekakshara, Akshi, Avadhuta, Katharudra, Hridaya, Yogakundalini, Panchabrahma, Pranagnihotra, Varaha, Kalisantarana and Sarasvatirahasya — the peace-mantra is "May he protect us both."

For the sixteen Upanishads belonging to the Sama Veda — Kena, Chandogya, Aruni, Maitrayani, Maitreyi, Vajrasuchika, Yogachudamani, Vasudeva, Mahat, Sannyasa, Avyakta, Kundika, Savitri, Rudraksha, Jabaladarshana and Jabali — the peace-mantra is "May my limbs grow strong."

For the thirty-one Upanishads belonging to the Atharva Veda — Prashna, Mundaka, Mandukya, Atharvashiras, Atharvashikha, Brihajjabala, Nrisimhatapani, Naradaparivrajaka, Sita, Sharabha, Mahanarayana, Ramarahasya, Ramatapani, Shandilya, Paramahamsaparivrajaka, Annapurna, Suryatma, Pashupata, Parabrahma, Tripuratapana, Devibhavana, Brahmajabala, Ganapati, Mahavakya, Gopalatapani, Krishna, Hayagriva, Dattatreya and Garuda — the peace-mantra is "May we hear what is auspicious with our ears."

Seekers of liberation, endowed with the fourfold means, full of faith, having duly approached — with gifts in hand — a true teacher who is of good family, learned in the Vedas, affectionate toward the scriptures, straightforward, devoted to the good of all beings and an ocean of compassion, having studied the one hundred and eight Upanishads in due form, and having practised hearing, reflection and contemplation without interruption, on the exhaustion of prarabdha karma break through the three bodies, and, like the space in a pot freed from its limiting adjunct, attain fullness: this is bodiless liberation.

That alone is the liberation of isolation. Therefore even those dwelling in the world of Brahma, having heard the Vedanta from the mouth of Brahma and so forth, attain isolation together with him. Thus liberation of isolation is said to come by knowledge alone — not by works, Sankhya, Yoga, worship and the like. Thus the Upanishad.

Then Maruti again asked Sri Ramachandra: "What is this attainment (of liberation), or what is the purpose of attainment?" Sri Rama said: "For a person, bondage is a quality of the mind, marked by being a doer and an enjoyer, by pleasure, pain and so on, and it has the nature of affliction. Its cessation is liberation while living. Like the space in a pot freed from its limiting adjunct, bodiless liberation comes from the exhaustion of prarabdha karma. The one hundred and eight Upanishads are the authority for liberation while living and bodiless liberation. The purpose is the attainment of eternal bliss by the removal of the sufferings of being a doer and the like. That is to be accomplished by human effort: as a son by the son-desiring sacrifice, wealth by trade and the like, heaven by the Jyotishtoma, so liberation while living and the rest are gained by the absorption produced by hearing the Vedanta and the like, which is accomplished by human effort. That is gained through the destruction of all latent tendencies. On this there are verses: 'Human effort is held to be of two kinds: contrary to scripture and in accord with scripture. The one contrary to scripture is for harm; the one in accord with scripture is for the highest good.'"
Through the habit-impressions of the world, of the scriptures, and of the body, knowledge does not arise in a creature as it should.
The array of habit-impressions is of two kinds, good and bad. If you are led there by the pure flood of impressions —
then by that very course quickly attain my state. But if an evil tendency involves you in distress —
one from earlier times — then that must be conquered by you with effort, monkey. The river of habit-impressions flows along the two courses, good and bad;
it should be directed to the good path by human effort. What has entered the bad one should bring down only to the good.
Moved away from the bad it goes to the good, and from that too to the other (state). By human effort one should tend the child that is the mind.
When, through the power of practice, the rise of a good habit-impression quickly comes to you, then know, destroyer of foes, that your practice has borne fruit.
Even when in great doubt, practise only the good. There is no harm, son of the Wind, in the growth of good habit-impressions.
The destruction of habit-impressions, knowledge, and the destruction of the mind, O wise one, are held to be fruitful when practised together for a long time.
As long as these three are not practised together, again and again, the state is not reached even in hundreds of years.
If they are practised one by one, even for a very long time, they do not give success, like mantras that are merely recited.
By these three practised for long, the firm knots of the heart snap without fail, like the fibres of a lotus stalk when it is cut.
The false habit-impression of worldly life, practised through hundreds of births, is nowhere destroyed without long practice.
Therefore, gentle one, by effort and human energy, discerningly, having abandoned the desire for enjoyment from afar, take refuge in these three alone.

Therefore the wise know the mind joined with habit-impressions as bound; the mind that has fully abandoned them is called free. Quickly practise the freedom of the mind from habit-impressions, great monkey.
By right reflection on the truth, habit-impression dissolves; when habit-impression dissolves, the mind becomes calm like a lamp.
He who, having abandoned habit-impression, stands undistracted in me, whose form is pure consciousness — he is I, of the nature of being, consciousness and bliss.
Whether he practises absorption or does his duties, or not — one whose heart has given up all striving is indeed free, of the highest disposition.
For one whose mind is free of habit-impressions, there is no purpose in inaction, none in actions, none in means or recitation.
For one who has abandoned habit-impressions, there is no higher state than silence.
Even without habit-impression, the eye and the other senses of themselves go outward toward their own objects; habit-impression is only the cause (in the ordinary case).
As the eye falls without attachment on visible things that come to it without effort, so does the steady-minded one act in his duties.
Sages know habit-impression, Maruti, as the awareness of existence made manifest and shaped accordingly, which ceases when the mind arises.
From the contemplation of a single object firmly practised, the exceedingly restless mind arises — the cause of birth, old age and death.
By force of habit-impression comes the stirring of the breath, and by that, again, habit-impression; thus the seed of the mind is made to sprout in the order of seed and shoot.
The mind-tree has two seeds: the stirring of the breath and habit-impression. When one of them is exhausted, both quickly perish.

Through conduct free from attachment, by giving up the imagining of worldly existence, and by seeing the destruction of the body, habit-impression does not arise. By abandoning habit-impressions the mind goes to the state of no-mind.
When, because of the absence of habit-impressions, the mind constantly does not think, then arises the state of no-mind, which bestows supreme peace.
As long as your mind is unripe and you do not know that state, act as determined by the authority of the teacher and the scriptures.
Then, with impurities ripened and the reality surely known, even that good flood of habit-impressions should be given up by you, free from anxiety.
The destruction of the mind is of two kinds: with form and without form. With form belongs to one liberated while living; without form, to one who has gone to bodiless liberation.

Listen now respectfully, pure one, to the destruction of this. When the state called the destruction of mind is present in you again, the mind endowed with qualities such as friendliness attains peace, without doubt; the mind of one liberated while living is freed from further birth.
This destruction of mind, with form, belongs to one liberated while living; the destruction of mind without form belongs to one who has gone to bodiless liberation.
(This world-tree,) splendid with a thousand shoots, branches, fruits and leaves —
of this tree of worldly existence the mind is the root; that, I think, is intention itself; by the quieting of intention, that (root) —
dry it up quickly, so that the tree of worldly existence withers. There is only one means: the restraint of one's own mind.
The rise of the mind is destruction; the destruction of the mind is the great rise. The mind of the knower goes to destruction; for the ignorant, the mind is a chain.
Until the mind is conquered by firm practice of the one truth, habit-impressions prance in the heart like ghouls in the night.
For one whose mental pride has withered and who has subdued the enemies that are the senses, the habit-impressions of enjoyment wither like lotuses in winter.
Pressing hand with hand, crushing teeth with teeth, overpowering limbs with limbs, one should first conquer one's own mind.
By a thinker sitting again and again in one place, the mind cannot be conquered without a blameless method.
As a vicious, rutting elephant is uncontrolled without a goad, so is the mind without these: study of the science of the Self, company of the good,
abandonment of habit-impressions, and restraint of the stirring of the breath — these are the well-established means for conquering the mind.
When these means exist, those who restrain the mind by force cast away the lamp and search for darkness with collyrium.
The deluded who set out to conquer the mind by force bind a mad king of elephants with lotus fibres.
There are two seeds of the mind-tree, the support of the creeper of mental activity: one is the stirring of the breath; the second is firm imagination.
That all-pervading awareness is moved by the stirring of the breath; therefore, from concentration of the mind, the knowledge that has been spoken of arises.
Now meditation, the means to that, is taught in due order. Even without any modification, by the reverse order of arising, contemplate pure consciousness, bliss of consciousness.
When the in-breath has set within and the out-breath has not yet risen in the heart, that state is experienced by yogis as retention (kumbhaka).
When the breath has set outside and the in-breath has not yet risen, that state of fullness is known as external retention.
The flow of the mind's activity in the form of Brahman, without the sense of "I," is cognitive absorption (samprajnata samadhi), through the excellence of the practice of meditation.
The mind whose activities have become quiet, giving supreme bliss — this absorption, called non-cognitive (asamprajnata), is dear to yogis.
Empty of light, empty of mind, empty of intellect, of the nature of consciousness — this absorption, whose nature is the exclusion of all that is not That, is contemplated by sages.
Full above, full below, full in the middle, of the nature of Shiva — this absorption is the absorption of ultimate truth, directly the face of the injunction.
The acceptance of an object through firm imagination, having abandoned reflection on before and after, is called habit-impression.
By what one has contemplated with intense fervour, one quickly becomes that very thing, best of monkeys, when free of every other habit-impression.
A person of that kind, overpowered by habit-impression, is deluded when he sees this as "true reality."
Because of the variety of the force of habit-impressions, one does not abandon one's own nature; the one of bad vision sees everything as confused, as if under the influence of intoxication.
Habit-impression is said to be of two kinds: pure and impure. The impure is the cause of birth; the pure destroys birth.
The impure habit-impression, dense with ignorance and full of dense egoism, is said by the wise to cause rebirth. Having abandoned the sprout of rebirth, one stays like a roasted seed.
What is the use of chewing over the patchwork of many scripture-stories in vain? The inner light should be sought with effort, Maruti.
Having abandoned seeing and not-seeing, he who abides by himself in his pure nature, tiger among monkeys, is Brahman; he himself is a knower of Brahman.
Having studied the four Vedas and all the scriptures many times, one does not know the truth of Brahman, as the ladle does not know the taste of the food.
If a man is not made dispassionate by the foul smell of his own body, what other cause of dispassion could be taught to him?
The body is utterly impure, the embodied one utterly pure; knowing the difference between the two, whose purification is prescribed?
The bound one is bound by habit-impression; liberation is the destruction of habit-impression. Having abandoned habit-impression, abandon also the desire for liberation.
Having first given up the habit-impressions of the mind that concern the objects of sense, take up the pure ones called friendliness and the like.
Having abandoned even these, though dealing with them, be inwardly at peace, equal in affection, with the impression of pure consciousness alone.
Then, having abandoned even that, which belongs to the mind and intellect, with the remainder steady and composed, be yourself in me, Maruti.

Without sound, without touch, without form, imperishable, also without taste, eternal, and without smell, without name and lineage — such is my form; worship it always, son of the Wind, destroyer of sorrow.
Of the nature of the seer, like space, supreme, shining once, unborn, one, imperishable, unsullied, all-pervading, without a second — that I am, entirely free.
I am the pure seer, of unchanging nature; by nature I have no object whatever. In front, across, above, below, everywhere — contemplate here: "I am the fully complete fullness."
Unborn, deathless, ageless, immortal, self-luminous, all-pervading, imperishable — I am; beyond cause and effect, stainless, ever satisfied — contemplate here: "I am that."
Having abandoned the state of liberation while living, when the body has been given to time, one enters bodiless liberation, as the wind enters stillness.
Of this a verse says:
The wise always see that supreme abode of Vishnu, like an eye spread out in the sky.
The wise, the vigilant, the inspired, kindle that supreme abode of Vishnu.
Om. Truth — thus the Upanishad. Om. That is full; this is full; from the full the full arises. Taking the full from the full, the full alone remains.
